content: Dr. Martin J. Llewelyn, a professor of infectious diseases at Brighton and Sussex Medical School, has critically examined the long-standing belief that completing an antibiotic course, even after symptoms resolve, is essential to prevent the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains. This belief originated in the 1940s during the early development of antibiotics. Notably, Alexander Fleming, in his Nobel Prize speech, warned that insufficient penicillin treatment for streptococcal throat infections could lead to the spread of resistant bacterial strains. However, Dr. Llewelyn points out that streptococci responsible for throat infections have not developed resistance to penicillin despite decades of use. Antibiotic resistance arises through two primary mechanisms: targeted selection and collateral selection. Targeted selection occurs when bacteria, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, develop resistance due to inadequate or single-agent antibiotic therapy. This mechanism accounts for a minority of resistance cases. In contrast, collateral selection, which is the predominant mechanism, occurs when antibiotics disrupt the normal bacterial flora in the body, creating an environment that allows resistant bacterial strains to thrive. Importantly, collateral selection is not influenced by the duration of antibiotic therapy. The relationship between the duration of antibiotic treatment and the development of resistance remains poorly studied. For most bacterial infections, the efficacy of conventional antibiotic courses has not been rigorously compared to shorter courses in terms of both clinical outcomes and the emergence of resistance. For example, pyelonephritis, traditionally treated with quinolones for two weeks, has been shown in trials to respond equally well to a 5-7 day course. Similarly, shorter antibiotic courses for otitis media have demonstrated comparable clinical outcomes to longer courses, with the added benefit of lower recurrence rates. In the case of hospital-acquired pneumonia, research suggests that shorter antibiotic courses may reduce the likelihood of future resistance development. Notably, none of these studies have found an association between shorter antibiotic courses and increased resistance. Dr. Llewelyn advocates for a more individualized approach to antibiotic prescribing. In hospitalized patients, he suggests using infection biomarkers, such as procalcitonin, to guide treatment duration. For outpatients, he recommends basing treatment on the patient’s symptoms. He also proposes reconsidering and revising the traditional message of “completing the course” of antibiotics. However, he emphasizes that further research is needed to validate these recommendations and fully understand the implications of shorter antibiotic courses on resistance development.
